title: Choosing a path: cost, data, and vendor constraints

opening.headline: Given budget, data volume, and vendor constraints, make an informed decision about what to do first among prompts, searches, and tuning.
body: The most common mistake when choosing an improvement path is to start with the method that seems the most powerful. But your budget is limited, you only have a few dozen examples to learn from, and you may not be sure if your vendor offers tuning.

In this lesson, we explore the decision flow starting with diagnosis and moving through prompts, searches, and tuning. We compare costs, data requirements, and vendor constraints for each route, explain alternatives when tuning is not possible, and even outline how to provide a basis for choice.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Failure cases, data volume, and budget can be classified as route selection criteria.
You can determine the basis for choosing the least cost path

screens.title: Within budget and vendor constraints, what to start with?
screens.lead: A team faces three candidate paths and three constraints. Read the situation and think about what more information you need.

visual.alt: Scene showing three constraint chips on the top and three candidate route cards on the bottom.
labels: Vendor: Unsure whether tuning is available

paragraphs: A team must improve the quality of model responses. There are three candidates: Prompt Improvement, Search Augmentation, and Tuning. However, the budget is limited, and there are only a few dozen human-made training examples. Additionally, I'm not sure if the vendor I'm using offers tuning.

OpenAI's Accuracy Optimization Guide summarizes three reasons why optimization is difficult: It is difficult to know how to start, what to use and when to use it, and what level of accuracy is necessary to use it in practice. This team's concerns encompass all three of these issues.

Without criteria for selection, meetings tend to end up with the most vocal opinion. This class covers a framework for selecting the least cost path based on failure type, cost, data requirements, and vendor constraints, and documenting the reasons.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Which of the three candidates is the lowest cost, and are there any cases where it might be okay to skip that path?

screens.outro: First, let's think about how your team sets priorities.

screens.title: Think about how you prioritize improvements
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about your team's approach first and then press it.

items.prompt: How do you prioritize improvement work?
items.answer: Each team has a different approach. What is important is whether you can explain what criteria your priorities came from. In this class, you will learn how to establish priorities around two criteria: failure type and cost.

items.prompt: What do you look at first: number of failures, cost, or schedule?
items.answer: All three are needed, but the first thing to look at is the type of failure case. This is because the path that can be used varies depending on whether there is a lack of information or behavioral instability. Cost and schedule are used to determine order among possible routes.

items.prompt: Did you make your decision based on evidence, or was it just intuition?
items.answer: Intuition can be a starting point, but if the evidence is not recorded, the same discussion will be repeated in the next judgment. At the end of this lesson, we introduce a simple record format for leaving evidence.

screens.outro: Now that we've got our thoughts in order, let's start by looking at the overall shape of the decision flow.

screens.title: Decision flow from diagnosis, prompting, discovery, and tuning
screens.lead: By selecting a number marker, you can see the decision questions and rationale being asked by each node. Please press them in order starting from 1.

visual.alt: A vertical flow chart that diagnoses failure through evaluation, determines the axis, selects the lever, and reevaluates it.
labels: Tuning after improving examples and instructions
Apply only one lever at a time

markers.label: diagnosis
markers.title: Evaluation creates baselines and causes of failure
markers.body: The first step is to create an evaluation baseline before using any levers. The OpenAI documentation instructs you to first write an evaluation that measures the output, followed by a prompt to produce the output to get a baseline. The Anthropic document also explains that success criteria should be specific and measurable. The output of this step is a failure example and a hypothesis about its cause.

markers.label: Axis judgment
markers.title: Determine whether it is a context problem or a behavioral problem
markers.body: For each failure, it asks whether the required information was present in the input. If there is no information, it is the context axis. If there is information but the method is shaky, it is the action axis. Only after making this decision can you decide which direction to take.

markers.label: Lever selection
markers.title: Choose a lever that matches your axis
markers.body: If you lack context, search will fill in the information you need. If the behavior is unstable, give clear instructions and show an example. If it is still repeated, go to tuning. This is a procession, not a straight staircase. Depending on the type of failure, the space you go to first will vary.

markers.label: one at a time
markers.title: Apply only one lever at a time
markers.body: If you change multiple levers at the same time, you won't know which change had an effect. Only apply one at a time so you can compare the effectiveness and cost of that lever. This is why the lever with the lowest cost is used first.

markers.label: reassess
markers.title: Check the extent of improvement through the same evaluation
markers.body: Measure again with the same assessment set to see how much improvement you have made. If the improvement is sufficient, stop, and if it is insufficient, re-diagnose the remaining failures. The evaluation results of each step become the basis for the next step. The OpenAI documentation describes this process as a continuously repeating cycle.

screens.outro: Now that we have the flow, let's look at three criteria for comparing paths: cost, data, and vendor.

screens.title: Cost order, data needs, vendor constraints
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the three paths based on cost, data needs, and vendor constraints.

tabs.label: cost order
tabs.body:
Typically, adoption costs increase in the following order: prompts, discovery, and tuning.

**Prompt**: Cheapest and fastest. Just change the wording and re-evaluate.

**Search**: An indexing infrastructure is needed to divide knowledge into chunks, embed them, and store them, and search quality must also be managed separately.

**Tuning**: You need to prepare the training data and run the training job. According to Google Cloud documentation, the number of training tokens is calculated by multiplying the number of tokens in the dataset by the number of epochs, and there is a separate cost for inference with the tuned model.

This order is a general trend, with failure types filtering out paths first, followed by cost.

tabs.label: data needs
tabs.body:
**Prompt**: A few examples and about 20 assessment questions are all you need to get started.

**Search**: You need the knowledge itself to be searched, as well as evaluation questions to check if the search is successful.

**Tuning**: OpenAI's map fine-tuning document sets the minimum number of examples that can be provided as 10, and explains that improvements are seen with 50 to 100 examples. I recommend starting with 50 well-made examples and evaluating them. If 50 doesn't work, there's also guidance to rethink the task or prompt before adding data.

So, if there are still dozens of examples, it makes sense to overhaul the prompts and evaluations before attempting tuning.

tabs.label: vendor constraints
tabs.body:
Even if the goal is the same, the possible paths vary depending on the vendor.

**Gemini API**: Google documentation indicates that models no longer support tuning in Gemini API and AI Studio, and that tuning is supported in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

**Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform**: Map fine-tuning is suitable when there are well-defined tasks and labeled data, and has established specifications, such as the total input and output of one training example cannot exceed 131,072 tokens.

**OpenAI**: The fine tuning platform is not open to new users, only existing users can create training jobs, the document states.

Whether the vendor offers tuning is the first thing to check before deciding on a route.

screens.outro: Now that you understand the constraints, let's explain alternatives in cases where tuning is not possible.

screens.title: Commentary: Alternatives when vendor does not provide tuning
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates the process of opening alternative paths one by one under constraints. Select the right arrow to skip a step. Learners do not enter answers.

steps.title: sort out the situation
steps.body: The API the team primarily uses does not support tuning. The problem is that the output format of the response is often shaky, and the information I need is already in the input. Since there is information, it is a problem on the action axis, and tuning would be a candidate. However, that path is not available on this vendor.

steps.title: Step 1: Make instructions clear and fix the action as much as possible with a few shots.
steps.body: Even if tuning is not possible, we do not give up on behavioral problems. Be specific about the format you want, and provide examples of the correct output in the prompt. The OpenAI documentation explains that adding static few-shot examples should improve consistency. It's the lowest cost, so we'll be the first to finish.

steps.title: Step 2: Dynamically load examples to fit the question
steps.body: If static examples are not enough, add a search step to retrieve examples related to your question on the fly. The representative flow of the OpenAI guide is a static few-shot followed by a search step that dynamically inserts examples. Instead of using the same example for every question, use examples that resemble the question, resulting in greater consistency. There are new indexing costs for search.

steps.title: Step 3: If it is still not enough, review places that support tuning
steps.body: If you've verified the previous two steps through evaluation and are still not meeting your goals, then look at other vendors or platforms that support tuning. For example, Gemini models support tuning on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The cost of moving will be justified only if you exhaust the first two steps first.

steps.title: Leave evidence through evaluation at every stage
steps.body: At the end of each phase, we measure improvement using the same set of assessments and record the results. Only with this record can you say based on whether to move on to the next step or stop here. Vendor constraints only block the path, they don't stop improvement itself. For example, if you have greatly reduced the number of failures in step 1, you can stop at the cost of indexing step 2, and this is what we really mean by choosing the least cost path. Conversely, if you go through both steps and still don't reach your evaluation goals, that record provides a valid basis for considering another vendor.

screens.outro: Now that we've solved the alternatives, let's see how we can finally base our choice.

screens.title: choice to leave a basis
screens.lead: Below is an example of a record that provides the basis for route selection. The description on the right tells you what each line contains and what happens if you leave it out.

data.code:
failure_type: behavior_instability
evidence: "JSON key name changed in 11 out of 30 evaluation sets"
chosen_path: few_shot_prompt
alternatives:
  - dynamic_few_shot_retrieval
  - fine_tuning
reasons:
  cost: "Prompt modification is the cheapest and fastest"
  data: "There are only 40 examples of correct answers, so it is still too early to start tuning."
  vendor: "Currently the API does not support tuning"
re_evaluation:
  result: "Reduced from 11 to 4"
  next_step: "Try dynamic example search"

notes.note: Types of failure and their evidence. If you don't write down the type of failure, you'll end up choosing a path without being able to distinguish between lack of information or behavioral instability, and evidence without numbers won't allow you to compare improvements later.
The path chosen and the alternatives examined. By writing down your alternatives together, if you get stuck on your chosen path, you can move on to the next candidate without discussing it again.

Write down the reasons for your choice by dividing them into cost, data volume, and vendor constraints. When reasons are mixed together, it is difficult to determine whether a choice should be revisited when conditions change.
Results of re-evaluation and next steps. If you don't keep track of your improvements, you'll be left with a feel for whether to continue your current path or change it.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed your recording habits, we will organize the entire class on the last screen.

screens.title: Starting with the cheapest route, with evidence
screens.lead: The initial question is to organize the criteria for what to do within budget and vendor constraints.

paragraphs: The order of choosing a route can be summarized as follows. First, failures are diagnosed by evaluation, failure types filter out paths, and the remaining candidates are applied one at a time, starting with the lowest cost path. The results of the assessment determine next steps.

Data volume and vendor constraints determine whether tuning is possible. If there are dozens of examples, overhaul the prompts and assessments first. If the vendor does not provide tuning, write down the prompts and search alternatives first. Still, I look into places that support tuning only when needed.

Finally, for every choice, we keep a record of the type of failure, the path and alternative chosen, the reasons, and the results of the reevaluation. Well-founded choices are also easier to revisit when conditions change. The record does not need to be long, four entries will suffice.

callout.label: Based on one sentence
callout.text: Starting with the cheapest route, select them one at a time based on failure type and evaluation results.

checks.intro: Think back to the decision flow you just saw and check for yourself. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: What does it mean to view the optimization path as a matrix rather than a straight staircase of ‘prompt, search, tune’?
options: All three steps must be completed in order.
The place to go first varies depending on the type of failure.
Search can only be used after the prompt ends.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The expression matrix means that the failure type determines the starting point.
checks.incorrectFeedback: That interpretation is incorrect. Consider again whether the word matrix enforces order or leaves choice open.
checks.explain: If the context is insufficient, search, and if the behavior is unstable, go to tuning after improving examples and instructions. The type of failure sets the path and the evaluation sets the next steps.

wrong.0: The term matrix means that the order is not enforced.
wrong.1: Tuning is an expensive step and is usually left behind.
wrong.3: Search and prompts are levers that solve different problems.

checks.intro: Think of the cost factors you compared in the tab and pair them with your route. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match a route with its cost factors
checks.correctFeedback: The cost factors of all three routes were adjusted appropriately.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some pairs were mismatched. Think again about which paths require new infrastructure or training tasks.
checks.explain: Prompts are the cheapest and fastest, search requires indexing infrastructure, and tuning requires data preparation and learning.

checks.intro: Try to remember the order of the alternative routes you saw in the commentary. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Order alternative steps for when your preferred API does not support tuning.
items: Make instructions clear and anchor actions with few-shot examples
Increase consistency by dynamically loading examples to fit the question.
If tuning is absolutely necessary, review vendors that support tuning.
checks.correctFeedback: I started with the lowest-cost alternative and reviewed the vendor at the end.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Recall the principle of trying the lowest cost route first.
checks.explain: If there are vendor constraints, exhaust the prompts and search alternatives first, then look at other vendors only when necessary. Confirm with evaluation at every step.

glossary.def: This is the process of deciding which lever to use among prompt, search, and tuning depending on the type of failure.
Prompts, search, and tuning are generally the orders of magnitude in increasing cost of adoption.
The amount and quality of examples and documentation required for each route. Tuning requires at least 10 examples and we recommend starting with 50 and evaluating.
The range of features provided by the platform you are using. Even if the goal is the same, the possible paths vary depending on the vendor.

misconceptions.myth: Tuning is always the final solution.
misconceptions.fact: There are many cases that can be solved with just prompts and searches. Tuning is a step that is reviewed after identifying limitations through evaluation.

misconceptions.myth: If the vendor doesn't provide tuning, improvement is impossible.
misconceptions.fact: Instructions, examples, and searches can significantly improve behavior and context. If it still isn't enough, look into places that support tuning.

misconceptions.myth: The order is a fixed staircase.
misconceptions.fact: It is a matrix determined by failure type, and the evaluation results determine the next steps.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Choose the cheapest route with rationale.
Failure type filters the path and evaluation determines the next steps.
Data volume and vendor constraints determine whether tuning is possible.
If there are vendor constraints, write out prompts and search alternatives first.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What failure types and evaluation results are the paths we use now based on?
